$$\Lambda(t) = \int_0^t \Lambda(ds) = \int_0^t \frac{P_1(ds)}{\bar{P}(s-)} = \phi^*(P_1, \bar{P})$$

$$\dot{\phi}^*_1(h_1) = \frac{d}{d\varepsilon} \phi^*(P_1 + \varepsilon h_1, \bar{P})|_{\varepsilon = 0}$$

$$\dot{\phi}^*_2(\bar{h}) = \frac{d}{d\varepsilon} \phi^*(P_1, \bar{P} + \varepsilon \bar{h})|_{\varepsilon = 0}$$

$$\frac{d}{d\varepsilon} \phi^*(P_1 + \varepsilon h_1, \bar{P}) = \frac{d}{d\varepsilon} \int_0^t \frac{(P_1 + \varepsilon h_1)(ds)}{\bar{P}(s-)} = \int_0^t \frac{h_1(ds)}{\bar{P}(s-)}$$

$$\frac{d}{d\varepsilon} \phi^*(P_1, \bar{P} + \varepsilon \bar{h})|_{\varepsilon=0} = \frac{d}{d\varepsilon} \int_0^t \frac{P_1(ds)}{(\bar{P} + \varepsilon \bar{h})(s-)}|_{\varepsilon=0}$$

$$= -\int_0^t \frac{P_1(ds)}{\{(\bar{P} + \varepsilon \bar{h})(s-)\}^2} \cdot \bar{h}(s-)|_{\varepsilon=0} = -\int_0^t \frac{\bar{h}(s-)P_1(ds)}{\{\bar{P}(s-)\}^2}$$

$$\dot{\phi}^*_2(\bar{P}_n - \bar{P}) = -\int_0^t (\bar{P}_n - \bar{P})(s-) \frac{P_1(ds)}{\{\bar{P}(s-)\}^2} = -\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \int_0^t I(\tilde{T}_i \ge s) \frac{P_1(ds)}{\{\bar{P}(s-)\}^2} + \int_0^t \frac{P_1(ds)}{\bar{P}(s-)}$$

$$= \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n IC^*(\tilde{T}_i, \Delta_i | P_1, \bar{P})$$

## Estimation of Influence Curve of Kaplan Meier using functional derivative
3/15/04  
Joseph Poj Gavinlertvatana

**Objective:**  
Derive the influence curve for Kaplan-Meier estimate by writing Kaplan-Meier minus truth as functional derivative of empirical minus truth in first order

Recall setup:  
Observe: $(\tilde{T} = \min(T, c), \Delta = I(T \le c))$, assume $T \perp c$

Parameter of interest:  
$$S(t) = P(T \ge t) = \prod_{s \in (0,t)} \left( 1 - \frac{\partial p_1(s)}{\bar{p}(s-)} \right)$$  
where $p_1(t) = P(\tilde{T} \le t, \Delta = 1)$ and $\bar{p}(t) = P(\tilde{T} > t)$  
$S(t) = \Phi(p_1, p_n)$ estimated by $S_n(t_0) = \Phi(p_{1n}, \bar{p}_n)$

Recall when we did directional derivative last time:  
$\Phi(p_1, p_n) = \Phi_2[\Phi_1(p_1, p_n)]$  
where $\Phi_1(p_1, p_n) = \int_0^\cdot \frac{\partial p_1(s)}{\bar{p}(s-)} = \Lambda(\cdot)$  
and $\Phi_2(\Lambda) = \prod_{s \in (0, t_0)} (1 - \partial \Lambda(s))$

$\Phi(p_1, p_n)$ maps data into cumulative hazard  
$\Phi_2(\Lambda)$ maps cumulative hazard into survival

For influence curve, we need to find the directional deriv:  
$$\dot{\Phi}(h_1, \bar{h}) = \frac{\partial}{\partial \varepsilon} \Phi(p_1 + \varepsilon h_1, \bar{p} + \varepsilon \bar{h})$$

Since $\Phi(p_1, p_n)$ is a composite function, we use the chain rule:  
$$\dot{\Phi}(h_1, \bar{h}) = \dot{\Phi}_2[\dot{\Phi}_1(h_1, \bar{h})]$$  
where $\dot{\Phi}_1(h_1, \bar{h}) = \frac{\partial}{\partial \varepsilon} \Phi_1(p_1 + \varepsilon h_1, \bar{p} + \varepsilon \bar{h})|_{\varepsilon=0} = \int_0^t \frac{h_1(\partial s)}{\bar{p}(s-)} - \int_0^t \frac{\bar{h}(s-) p_1(\partial s)}{[\bar{p}(s-)]^2}$  
and $\dot{\Phi}_2(g) = \frac{\partial}{\partial \varepsilon} \Phi_2(\Lambda + \varepsilon g)|_{\varepsilon=0}$

To get $\dot{\Phi}_2(g)$, we use a telescoping trick  
e.g.  
$$a_1 a_2 - b_1 b_2 = (a_1 - b_1) b_2 + a_1 (a_2 - b_2)$$  
$$a_1 a_2 a_3 - b_1 b_2 b_3 = (a_1 - b_1) b_2 b_3 + a_1 (a_2 - b_2) b_3 + a_1 a_2 (a_3 - b_3)$$  
In general:

$$\prod_{j=1}^k a_j - \prod_{j=1}^k b_j = \sum_{j=1}^k [(\prod_{l=1}^{j-1} a_l) (a_j - b_j) (\prod_{l=j+1}^k b_l)]$$

Continuing, we get:  
$$\dot{\Phi}_2(g) = \lim_{\varepsilon \to 0} \frac{\Phi_2(\Lambda + \varepsilon g) - \Phi_2(\Lambda)}{\varepsilon}$$  
$$= \lim_{\varepsilon \to 0} \frac{\prod_{s \in (0,t_0)} [1 - (\Lambda + \varepsilon g)(s)] - \prod_{s \in (0,t_0)} [1 - \partial\Lambda(s)]}{\varepsilon}$$  
(using telescoping)  
$$= \lim_{\varepsilon \to 0} \frac{\int_{s \in (0,t_0)} [\prod_{u \in (0,s)} (1 - \partial(\Lambda + \varepsilon g)(u))][1 - \partial(\Lambda + \varepsilon g)(s) - 1 + \partial(\Lambda)(s)][\prod_{u \in (s,t_0)} (1 - \partial\Lambda(u))]}{\varepsilon}$$  
$$= \lim_{\varepsilon \to 0} - \int_{s \in (0,t_0)} [\prod_{u \in (0,s)} (1 - \partial(\Lambda + \varepsilon g)(u))][\partial g(s)][\prod_{u \in (s,t_0)} (1 - \partial\Lambda(u))]$$  
$$= - \int_{s \in (0,t_0)} [\prod_{u \in (0,s)} (1 - \partial(\Lambda)(u))][\partial g(s)][\prod_{u \in (s,t_0)} (1 - \partial\Lambda(u))]$$  
$$= - \int_{s \in (0,t_0)} \frac{\prod_{u \in (0,t_0)} (1 - \partial(\Lambda)(u))}{(1 - \partial(\Lambda)(s))} \partial g(s)$$  
$$= - \prod_{u \in (0,t_0)} (1 - \partial(\Lambda)(u)) \int_0^{t_0} \frac{\partial g(s)}{(1 - \partial(\Lambda)(s))}$$  
$$= -S(t_0) \int_0^{t_0} \frac{\partial g(s)}{(1 - \partial(\Lambda)(s))}$$  
If $\Lambda(s)$ is continuous, then $\partial\Lambda(s) = 0$, so  
$$= -S(t_0) g(t_0)$$

So by plugging in $g = \dot{\Phi}_1(h_1, \bar{h})$  
$$\dot{\Phi}(h_1, \bar{h}) = -S(t_0) \int_0^{t_0} \frac{\partial \dot{\Phi}_1(h_1, \bar{h})}{1 - \partial\Lambda(s)}$$  
$$= S(t_0) \int_0^{t_0} \frac{1}{1 - \partial\Lambda(s)} \left[ \frac{h_1(\partial s)}{\bar{p}(s-)} - \frac{\bar{h}(s-)}{\bar{p}^2(s-)} \partial p_1(s) \right]$$

So, finally, we can write Kaplan-Meier minus truth in first order:  
$$S_n(t_0) - S(t_0) \cong \dot{\Phi}(p_{1n} - p_1, \bar{p}_n - \bar{p})$$  
$$= -S(t_0) \left[ \int_0^{t_0} \frac{1}{\partial\Lambda(s)} \frac{\partial p_{1n}}{\bar{p}(s-)} - \int_0^{t_0} \frac{\bar{p}_n}{\bar{p}^2(s-)} \partial p_1(s) \right]$$  
$$= -S(t_0) \left[ \int_0^{t_0} \frac{1}{\partial\Lambda(s)} \frac{\partial(p_{1n} - p_1)}{\bar{p}(s-)} - \int_0^{t_0} \frac{1}{\partial\Lambda(s)} \frac{(\bar{p}_n - \bar{p})(s-)}{\bar{p}^2(s-)} \partial p_1(s) \right]$$

And we make this into a sample average:  
$$= \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n -S(t_0) \left[ \int_0^{t_0} \frac{1}{1 - \partial\Lambda(s)} \frac{\partial I(\tilde{T}_i \le s, \Delta_i = 1)}{\bar{p}(s-)} - \int_0^{t_0} \frac{1}{1 - \partial\Lambda(s)} \frac{I(\tilde{T}_i \ge s)}{\bar{p}^2(s-)} \partial p_1(s) \right]$$

Finally, we get the influence curve:  
$$S_n(t_0) - S(t_0) \cong \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n -S(t_0) \left[ \frac{I(\tilde{T}_i \le t_0, \Delta_i = 1)}{(1 - \partial\Lambda(\tilde{T}_i))\bar{p}(\tilde{T}_i-)} - \int_0^{\min(t_0, \tilde{T}_i)} \frac{1}{1 - \partial\Lambda(s)} \frac{\partial p_1(s)}{\bar{p}^2(s-)} \right]$$

recall that $\partial\Lambda(\tilde{T}_i) = \frac{\partial p_1(\tilde{T}_i)}{\bar{p}}$

## QUANTILE ESTIMATION BASED ON RIGHT-CENSORED DATA

**Data:**

$$(\tilde{T} = \min(T, C), \Delta = I(T \le C))$$

where $C \perp T$ ($C$ and $T$ are independent), $C \sim G$, $T \sim F$

**Parameter of interest:**

$$\theta(F) = F^{-1}(p), \text{ where } p \in (0, 1) \text{ and } F^{-1}(p) = \inf\{x : F(x) \ge p\}$$

**Estimation:**

$$F_n = 1 - S_n, \text{ and } S_n \text{ is Kaplan-Meier estimator. } \theta_n = \theta(F_n) = F_n^{-1}(p)$$

Now, how do we do the inference?  
We need to estimate IC.  
$\theta_n - \theta = \theta(F_n) - \theta(F) \cong \dot{\theta}(F_n - F)$ (using Delta Method)  
Take a directional derivative:  
$$\dot{\theta} = \frac{d}{d\varepsilon} \theta(F + \varepsilon \cdot h)|_{\varepsilon=0}$$  
For simplicity, let $F_\varepsilon = F + \varepsilon h$, $\theta_\varepsilon = \theta(F_\varepsilon)$, and $y = F(\theta_\varepsilon)$. Also, note that $F_\varepsilon(\theta_\varepsilon) = F(\theta_\varepsilon) + \varepsilon h(\theta_\varepsilon)$  
Then,

$$\dot{\theta} = \frac{d}{d\varepsilon} \theta(F + \varepsilon \cdot h)|_{\varepsilon=0}$$

$$\dot{\theta} = \lim_{\varepsilon \to 0} \frac{\theta(F_\varepsilon) - \theta(F)}{\varepsilon} = \lim_{\varepsilon \to 0} \frac{F_\varepsilon^{-1}(p) - F^{-1}(p)}{\varepsilon} = \lim_{\varepsilon \to 0} \left[ -\frac{F^{-1}F_\varepsilon(\theta_\varepsilon) - F^{-1}F(\theta_\varepsilon)}{\varepsilon} \right]$$

Substituting $y$ into the expression of limit, and using the fact that

$$F^{-1}(y + \varepsilon h) - F^{-1}(y) \cong \frac{d}{dy} F^{-1}(y) \cdot \varepsilon h$$

, we get

$$\dot{\theta}(h) = \lim_{\varepsilon \to 0} \left[ -\frac{F^{-1}(y + \varepsilon h(\theta_\varepsilon)) - F^{-1}(y)}{\varepsilon} \right] = \lim_{\varepsilon \to 0} \left[ -\frac{\frac{d}{dy} F^{-1}(y) \cdot \varepsilon h(\theta_\varepsilon)}{\varepsilon} \right]$$

$$= -\lim_{\varepsilon \to 0} \left. \frac{d}{dy} F^{-1}(y) \right|_{y=F(\theta_\varepsilon)} \cdot h(\theta_\varepsilon)$$

$$= -\left. \frac{d}{dy} F^{-1}(y) \right|_{y=F(\theta)} \cdot h(\theta)$$

$$= -\frac{1}{f(\theta)} h(\theta) = -\frac{1}{f(F^{-1}(p))} h(F^{-1}(p))$$

Note: Above we differentiated the inverse function.  
What is the derivative of $F^{-1}$?  
Recall:

$$F^{-1}(F(y)) = y$$

Differentiate both sides with respect to $y$:

$$\frac{d}{dy} F^{-1} F(y) = 1$$

Applying Chain Rule:

$$(F^{-1})'(F(y)) \cdot F'(y) = 1, \text{ note: } F'(y) \equiv f(y)$$

So,

$$(F^{-1})'(F(y)) = \frac{1}{f(y)}$$

Thus,

$$(F^{-1})'(z) = \frac{1}{f(F^{-1}(z))}$$

**Now we are ready for the influence curve.**  
Applying the first order Taylor expansion:

$$\theta_n - \theta \cong \frac{-1}{f(\theta)} (F_n - F)(\theta) = \frac{1}{f(\theta)} (S_n - S)(\theta)$$

$$\cong \frac{1}{f(\theta)} \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n IC_{KM}(\tilde{T}_i, \Delta_i | \theta)$$

$$= \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{1}{f(\theta)} IC_{KM}(\tilde{T}_i, \Delta_i | \theta)$$

$$= \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{-1}{f(\theta)} S(\theta) \left[ \frac{I(\tilde{T}_i, \Delta_i = 1)}{\bar{p}(\theta)} - \int_0^{\min(\theta, \tilde{T}_i)} \frac{dP_1(S)}{\bar{P}^2(S)} \right]$$

$$f_n(\theta) = \frac{F_n(\theta + h) - F_n(\theta - h)}{2h}$$

(Another way to construct confidence interval is to use bootstrap method. However, there are situations when the bootstrap method fails.)

## SELF-CONSISTENCY EQUATION FOR CENSORED DATA

$X \sim F_n$, $C | X \sim G(\cdot | X)$ where distribution function $G$ is called a censoring mechanism.  
We observe: $Y = \phi(C, X) \sim P_{F_X, G}$  
A random set $C(Y)$ is called a coarsening of $X$ if $Pr(X \in C(Y)) = 1$  
(1)

$$Y = (\tilde{T}, \Delta)$$

$$C(\tilde{T}, \Delta) = \begin{cases} \{\tilde{T}\}, \text{ if } \Delta = 1 \\ (\tilde{T}, \infty), \text{ if } \Delta = 0 \end{cases}$$

(2)

$$Y = (C, I(T < C))$$

$$C(\tilde{T}, \Delta) = \begin{cases} (-\infty, C), \text{ if } \Delta = 1 \\ (C, \infty), \text{ if } \Delta = 0 \end{cases}$$

We say $C(Y)$ satisfies coarsening at random (CAR) if  
$Pr(X = x | Y = y) = Pr(X = x | X \in C(y))$.  
Equivalently, $Pr(Y = y | X = x)$ is constant for $x \in C(y)$.  
Suppose we have $n$ iid: $Y_1, \ldots, Y_n$. We want to estimate $F_X(A) = Pr(X \in A)$.  
**Full data:**

$$F_{X,n} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n I(X_i \in A)$$

**Censored data:**

$$F_{X,n}(A) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n E[I(X_i \in A | Y_i)]$$

**Or**

$$F_{X,n}(A) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n E_{F_{X,n}} [I(X_i \in A | X_i \in C(Y_i))]$$

$$= \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n P_{F_{X,n}} (X_i \in A | X_i \in C(Y_i))$$

$$= \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{P_{X,n}(X_i \in A \cap C(Y_i))}{P_{F_{X,n}}(X \in C(Y_i))}$$

Thus,

$$F_{X,n}(A) = \underbrace{\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{P_{X,n}(X_i \in A \cap C(Y_i))}{P_{F_{X,n}}(X \in C(Y_i))}}_{\text{This is called a self-consistency equation}}$$

If we enforce $F_{X,n}$ to be discrete on $\{x_1, \ldots, x_m\}$ with point masses $p_{1n} \ldots p_{mn}$, then $p_{j,n} = P_{F_{X,n}}(X = x_j)$

$$p_{j,n} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{p_{j,n} I(x_i \in C(Y_i))}{\sum_{x_l \in C(Y_i)} p_{l,n}}$$

for $j = 1, \ldots, m$  
The following algorithm can be used to solve this equation:

$$p_{j,n}^{k+1} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{p_{j,n}^k I(x_i \in C(Y_i))}{\sum_{x_l \in C(Y_i)} p_{l,n}^k}$$

where the iteration start with $p^0 = (p_{1,n}^0, \ldots, p_{m,n}^0)$.

## Truncation
Notes by Keith Betts  
March 17, 2004

## Situation

Survival time $T$ has distribution $F$  
Truncation time $C^*$ has distribution $G^*$  
$T$ and $C^*$ are independent  
Observe $n$ i.i.d. observations of $(T', C^{*\prime})$ with distribution $(T, C^*) \mid T > C^*$  
We want to estimate $S(t) = Pr(T > t)$.

## Example

Population of HIV infected patients  
$T = T_{\text{Death}} - T_{\text{AIDS}}$  
$C^* = 1988 - T_{\text{AIDS}}$ where $C^* = 0$ if $T_{\text{AIDS}} > 1988$  
Sample is from $(T, C^*) \mid T > C^*$

Define $P(s) = Pr(T' \ge s)$  
Define $\bar{P}(s) = Pr(T' \ge s, C^{*\prime} < s)$

$$S(t) = Pr(T > t) = \prod_{s \in (0,t)} 1 - \frac{Pr(T \in (s, s + ds))}{Pr(T \ge s)}$$

$$= \prod_{s \in (0,t)} 1 - \frac{Pr(T \in (s, s + ds), C^* < s)}{Pr(T \ge s, C^* < s)}$$

$$= \prod_{s \in (0,t)} 1 - \frac{Pr(T \in (s, s + ds), C^* < s \mid T > C^*)}{Pr(T \ge s, C^* < s \mid C^*)}$$

$$= \prod_{s \in (0,t)} 1 - \frac{Pr(T' \in (s, s + ds), C^{*\prime} < s)}{Pr(T' \ge s, C^{*\prime} < s)}$$

$$= \prod_{s \in (0,t)} 1 - \frac{Pr(T' \in (s, s + ds))}{Pr(T' \ge s, C^{*\prime} < s)}$$

$$= \prod_{s \in (0,t)} 1 - \frac{P(s)}{\bar{P}(s)}$$

$$\equiv \phi(P(s), \bar{P}(s))$$

Essentially, we have proved Identifiability.

Trouble arises if $\bar{P}(s) = Pr(T' \ge s, C^{*\prime} < s) = 0$  
This occurs if $C^* < s$ is never true.

Assuming that $Pr(C^* < s) > 0$ for $s \in (0, t)$, Identifiability is shown.

We now focus on the task of constructing estimators.  
Define $P_n(s) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n I(T_i' \le s)$  
Define $\bar{P}_n(s) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n I(T_i' \ge s, C_i^{*\prime} < s)$

We have shown that $S(t) = \phi(P, \bar{P})$  
Therefore, $S_n(t) = \phi(P_n, \bar{P}_n)$  
This is the Product Limit Estimator for truncated data.

We will now turn our attention to obtaining the Influence Curve.  
Using the Functional Delta Method:

$$S_n(t) - S(t) \approx \dot{\phi}(P_n - P, \bar{P}_n - \bar{P})$$

$$\text{where } \dot{\phi}(h, \bar{h}) = \left. \frac{d}{d\varepsilon} \phi(P + \varepsilon h, \bar{P} + \varepsilon \bar{h}) \right|_{\varepsilon=0} = -S(t) \left[ \int_0^t \frac{h(ds)}{\bar{P}(s)} - \int_0^t \frac{\bar{h}(s) dP(s)}{\bar{P}^2(s)} \right]$$

$$\text{Thus, } h = P_n - P, \bar{h} = \bar{P}_n - \bar{P}$$

$$S_n(t) - S(t) \approx \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n -S(t) \left[ \int_0^t I(T_i' \in (s, s + ds) - \int_0^t I(T_i' \ge s, C_i^{*\prime} < s) \frac{dP(s)}{\bar{P}^2(s)} \right]$$

$$\approx \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \underbrace{-S(t) \left[ \frac{I(T_i' \le t)}{\bar{P}(T_i')} - \int_0^t I(T_i' \ge s, C_i^{*\prime} < s) \frac{dP(s)}{\bar{P}^2(s)} \right]}_{IC(T_i', C_i^{*\prime}, \mid P, \bar{P}, t)}$$

## Truncation with Right Censoring

Assume:  
$T \perp (C, C^*)$  
$T \sim F$  
$C^* \sim G^*$  
$C \sim G$  
We observe $(\tilde{T} = \min(T, C), \Delta = I(T \le C), C^*)) \mid T > C^*, C > C^*$  
Where $(T', C', C^{*\prime})$ has distribution $(T, C, C^*) \mid T > C^*, C > C^*$  
Define $\tilde{T}' = \min(T', C')$ and $\Delta' = I(T' \le C')$

We want to estimate $S(t) = \Pr(T > t)$  
Express $S(t)$ as distribution of data based on $n$ i.i.d. $(\tilde{T}_i', \Delta_i', C_i^{*\prime})$ for $i = 1, \ldots, n$

$$S(t) = Pr(T > t) = \prod_{s \in (0,t)} \left( 1 - \frac{Pr(T = s)}{Pr(T \ge s)} \right)$$

$$= \prod_{s \in (0,t)} \left( 1 - \frac{Pr(T = s, C^* < s, C > s)}{Pr(T \ge s, C^* < s, C > s)} \right)$$

$$= \prod_{s \in (0,t)} \left( 1 - \frac{Pr(T = s, C^* < s, C > s \mid T > C^*, C > C^*)}{Pr(T \ge s, C^* < s, C > s \mid T > C^*, C > C^*)} \right)$$

$$= \prod_{s \in (0,t)} \left( 1 - \frac{Pr(\tilde{T}' = s, \Delta' = 1, C^{*\prime} < s)}{Pr(\tilde{T}' \ge s, C^{*\prime} < s)} \right)$$

$$\approx \phi(P_1, \bar{P})$$

$$\text{where } P_1(s) = Pr(\tilde{T}' \le s, \Delta' = 1)$$

$$\bar{P}(s) = Pr(\tilde{T}' \ge s, C^{*\prime} < s)$$

$$\text{Thus, } S(t) = \phi(P_1, \bar{P})$$

$$S_n(t) = \phi(P_{1n}, \bar{P}_n)$$

$$\text{where } P_{1n}(s) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n I(\tilde{T}_i' \le s, \Delta_i' = 1)$$

$$\text{and } \bar{P}_n(s) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n I(\tilde{T}_i' \le s, C_i^{*\prime} < s)$$

Using the Functional Delta Method

$$S_n(t) - S(t) \approx \dot{\phi}(P_{1n} - P_1, \bar{P}_{1n} - \bar{P}_1)$$

$$\text{where} \quad \dot{\phi}(h_1, \bar{h}) = -S(t) \left[ \int_0^t \frac{h_1(ds)}{\bar{P}(s)} - \int_0^t \frac{\bar{h}(s) dP(s)}{\bar{P}^2(s)} \right]$$

$$S_n(t) - S(t) \approx \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n -S(t) \left[ \int_0^t \frac{I(\tilde{T}_i' = s, \Delta_i' = 1)}{\bar{P}(s)} - \int_0^t I(\tilde{T}_i' \ge s, C_i^{*\prime} < s) \frac{dP_1(s)}{\bar{P}^2(s)} \right]$$

$$\approx \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \underbrace{-S(t) \left[ \int_0^t \frac{I(\tilde{T}_i' = s, \Delta_i' = 1)}{\bar{P}(T_i')} - \int_0^t I(\tilde{T}_i' \ge s, C_i^{*\prime} < s) \frac{dP_1(s)}{\bar{P}^2(s)} \right]}_{IC(T_i', C_i^{*\prime} \mid P_1, \bar{P}, t)}$$

## 3 The EM-Algorithm For Computing The MLE of a Full Data Model Based on Censored Data

Let $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n$ be $n$ i.i.d. observations drawn from a full data distribution $F_X$ with density $f_\theta$. Let the observed data $Y_1 = \phi(C_1, X_1), Y_2 = \phi(C_2, X_2), \ldots, Y_n = \phi(C_2, X_n)$ be $n$ i.i.d. observations $Y = \phi(C, X) \sim P_{f_\theta, G} \equiv P_{\theta, G}$, where the random variable $C$ represents the censoring on $X$ (note that $C$ and $X$ may not necessarily be univariate R.V.). Let $G \equiv G_{C|X}$ denote the censoring mechanism.

Let $C(Y)$ be the coarsening of $X$ implied by $Y$: $C_Y \equiv C(Y)$ is a subset of domain $(X)$ such that $\Pr(X \in C(Y)) = 1$. We'll assume for the rest of this lecture that $C_Y$ satisfies the so-called **Coarsening At Random (CAR)** condition: $\Pr(Y = y \mid X = x)$ is constant for $x \in C(Y)$. Alternatively the condition can be expressed as that the coarsening mechanism (i.e. the conditional density $g$ of the conditional distribution $G'(\cdot | X)$ of the observed data $Y$ given $X$) is CAR if it's a function of $Y$ only. In other words knowing what the value of the random variable $X$ is, does not in any way provide more info on the observed data $Y$, including the censoring mechanism $G$.

Assuming CAR, the likelihood for an individual observation factorizes into a part that depends on the censoring mechanism $G$ and a part that doesn't: $P_{\theta, G}(Y = y) = P_{f_\theta}(X \in C(Y)) P_G(Y = y \mid X = x)$. Hence, the log-likelihood of $Y_1, Y_2, \ldots, Y_n$ under CAR simplifies to:

$$\text{Loglik}(Y_1, Y_2, \ldots, Y_n \mid \theta, G) = \sum_{i=1}^n \log F_\theta(C(Y_i)) + \sum_{i=1}^n \log P_G(Y_i \mid X_i),$$

which is maximized by the MLE estimator:

$$\theta_n = \arg\max_\theta \sum_{i=1}^n \log F_\theta(C(Y_i)).$$

Note that $F_\theta(C(Y_i))$ is an alternative form for $\int_{C(Y)} f_\theta(x) dx$.

In the most general case, the model for $F_\theta$ is **non-parametric**, and $\theta_n$ is found using the **Expectation-Maximization algorithm**, or **EM-alg** for short, which is described below:

1. Initialize $\theta$ with some value $\theta^0$;

2. For $k = 1, 2, \ldots$ repeat until convergence:
   $$\theta^{k+1} = \arg\max_\theta E_{\theta^k} [\log f_\theta(X_1, \ldots, X_n) \mid Y_1, \ldots, Y_n].$$

The EM algorithm performs repeatedly two steps: first, for $\theta^k$ - fixed, the conditional expectation of the observed data log-likelihood is calculated, which simultaneously imputes the missing/censored data as well. This is followed by finding which value of $\theta$ maximizes the full-data likelihood using the newly imputed values of $X$ and setting the $\theta^{k+1}$ to that value.

The EM-alg always converges to a local maximum. In the case of $X$ being distributed with density from the exponential family of distributions:

$$f_\theta(x) = \exp[p(\theta) K(x) + S(x) + q(\theta)]$$

the EM-alg reduces to:

$$\theta^{k+1} = \arg\max_\theta \sum_{i=1}^n E_{\theta^k} [\log f_\theta(X_i) \mid X_i \in C(Y_i)]$$

$$= \arg\max_\theta \sum_{i=1}^n E_{\theta^k} [\log f_\theta(X_i) \mid Y_i]$$

$$= \arg\max_\theta \sum_{i=1}^n E_{\theta^k} [p(\theta) K(X_i) + S(X_i) + q(\theta) \mid Y_i]$$

$$= \arg\max_\theta \sum_{i=1}^n \{p(\theta) E_{\theta^k} [K(X_i) \mid Y_i] + E_{\theta^k} [S(X_i) \mid Y_i] + q(\theta)\}$$

$$= \arg\max_\theta \left( p(\theta) \sum_{i=1}^n E_{\theta^k} [K(X_i) \mid Y_i] + \sum_{i=1}^n E_{\theta^k} [S(X_i) \mid Y_i] + nq(\theta) \right)$$

$$= \arg\max_\theta \{p(\theta) K_n(Y_1, \ldots, Y_n) + S_n(Y_1, \ldots, Y_n) + nq(\theta)\},$$

where $K_n(Y_1, \ldots, Y_n) \equiv \sum_{i=1}^n E_{\theta^k} [K(X_i) \mid Y_i]$ and $S_n(Y_1, \ldots, Y_n) \equiv \sum_{i=1}^n E_{\theta^k} [S(X_i) \mid Y_i]$.  
Now, compare the above with the full data MLE based on $X_1, \ldots, X_n$:

$$\theta^{\text{Full}} = \arg\max_\theta \sum_{i=1}^n \log f_\theta(X_i)$$

$$= \arg\max_\theta \left( p(\theta) \sum_{i=1}^n K(X_i) + \sum_{i=1}^n S(X_i) + nq(\theta) \right)$$

$$= \arg\max_\theta \{p(\theta) K_n(X_1, \ldots, X_n) + S_n(X_1, \ldots, X_n) + nq(\theta)\},$$

where $K_n(X_1, \ldots, X_n) \equiv \sum_{i=1}^n K(X_i)$ and $S_n(X_1, \ldots, X_n) \equiv \sum_{i=1}^n S(X_i)$. Hence, in the case of distribution from the exponential family, knowing how to find the full data MLE directly translates in knowing how to find the observed data MLE: replace $K(X_i)$ with the conditional expectation $E_{\theta^k} [K(X_i) \mid Y_i]$ and iterate.

## NPMLE based on censored data

Let $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n$ be $n$ i.i.d. $X \sim F_X \in \mathcal{M}$, where $\mathcal{M}$ is non-parametric, and $Y_1, Y_2, \ldots, Y_n$ be $n$ i.i.d. observations $Y = \phi(C, X) \sim P_{F_X, G}$. Assume CAR on $G$. As in the case when we were dealing with finite dimensional real-valued parameter, we maximize the log-likelihood ratio of the observed data:

$$F_{X,n} = \arg\max_{F_X} \sum_{i=1}^n \log F_X(C(Y_i)).$$

Suppose we restrict to or know that $F_X$ domain is a finite and discrete set of points $\{x_1, \ldots, x_m\}$:  
$F_X \in \mathcal{D} = \left\{ p = (p_1, \ldots, p_m) : \sum_{j=1}^m p_j = 1 \right\}$. Hence, $F_X$ is a multinomial distribution $M(n, p_1, \ldots, p_m)$. Let $n_j = \sum_{i=1}^n I(X_i = x_j)$. Thus we can use the general EM-alg, because the multinomial distribution is a member of the exponential family of distributions.

1. In step $k = 0$ initialize $p^0 = (1/m, \ldots, 1/m)$;

2. For $k = 1, 2, \ldots$ until convergence:
   $$p^{k+1} = \arg\max_p E_{p^k} [\log f_p(n_1, \ldots, n_m) \mid Y_1, \ldots, Y_n]$$
   $$= \arg\max_p E_{p^k} \left[ \sum_{j=1}^m n_j \log p_j \mid Y_1, \ldots, Y_n \right]$$
   $$= \arg\max_p \sum_{j=1}^m E_{p^k} [n_j \mid Y_1, \ldots, Y_n] \log p_j.$$

Setting

$$\frac{\partial}{\partial p_j} \left( \sum_{j=1}^m E_{p^k} [n_j \mid Y_1, \ldots, Y_n] \log p_j \right) = 0,$$

and using the constraint $\sum p_j = 1$ leads to the following result:

$$p_j^{k+1} = \frac{1}{n} E_{p^k} [n_j \mid Y_1, \ldots, Y_n]$$

$$= \frac{1}{n} E_{p^k} \left[ \sum_{i=1}^n I(X_i = x_j) \mid Y_1, \ldots, Y_n \right]$$

$$= \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n P_{p^k}[X_i = x_j \mid Y_i]$$

$$= \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{P_{p^k}(X_i = x_j) I(x_j \in C(Y_i))}{\sum_l p_l^k I(x_l \in C(Y_i))}, \quad j = 1, \ldots, m$$

which is an example of a self-consistency equation introduced in the previous lecture.

NPMLE found using EM-alg is not necessarily consistent. One such interesting example is the NPLME of the bivariate survival function subject to censoring. Typically, this kind of problems arise in studies of twins with a certain disease. Let $T = (T_1, T_2)$ be the bivariate survival time of a randomly drawn twin pair from a population with unknown survival distribution $S_0$ to be estimated. Assume that each pair is subject to right censoring which will be denoted with $C = (C_1, C_2)$. For each twin we observe the minimum of the censoring and survival time, as well as if the observation is censored or not:

$$Y_i \equiv \left(\tilde{T}_i, D_i\right), \quad \tilde{T}_i = \left(\tilde{T}_{i1}, \tilde{T}_{i2}\right)^T, \quad D_i = I(T_{i1} \le C_{i1}, T_{i2} \le C_{i2}), \quad i = 1, \ldots, n.$$

The data can be thought of as occupying points, half-lines and quadrants in the plane as shown in fig. 1 below.

Assuming that the model for bivariate survival function is non-parametric, the NPMLE satisfies the self-consistency equations solved by the EM-alg. In the initialization step, the algorithm assigns mass of $1/n$ for each observation. Then for all censored pairs, i.e. those that are represented as half-lines and quadrants, their mass is redistributed over the associated region of coarsening $C(Y_i)$, according to an estimate of the conditional distribution which is obtained over all uncensored observations that fall into $C(Y_i)$. This is repeated with the new masses until the algorithm converges. If the time is on a continuous scale then the half-lines a.s. do not contain any (uncensored) observations, hence the conditional distribution for singly-censored observations can not be estimated properly, and as a consequence the NPMLE for bivariate right-censored data is inconsistent.

In series of papers Van der Laan [1994, 1995] proposed a way to repair the consistency of the NPMLE, by employing the following strategy: for each of the singly-censored observations replace the half-line with (half-)strip of width $h$ parallel to the half-line (as shown in the picture) and estimate the conditional distribution from all uncensored observations with bigger time-to-event than that of the singly-censored observation, hence allowing the EM-alg to redistribute the mass $1/n$ over such a half-strip. This estimator is asymptotically efficient when $h \to \infty$ and is asymptotically unbiased even if $h$ is fixed.

## What is an Estimating Function

Suppose that $X_1, \ldots, X_n \sim F_X \in \mathcal{M}$ iid, that $\mu(F_X) \in \mathbb{R}^k$ is a euclidean parameter of interest, and that $\eta(F_X)$ is a nuisance parameter. Then $D(X \mid \mu, \eta) \in \mathbb{R}^k$ is an estimating function if $E_{F_X}[D(X \mid \mu(F_X), \eta(F_X))] = 0$. That is, if the function evaluated at the true parameters has expectation zero. If $\hat{\eta}$ is an estimate of $\eta$, then the estimating function estimate of $\mu(F_X)$ is the $\mu_n$ solving $\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n D(X_i \mid \mu, \hat{\eta}) = 0$.

## Background on Tangent Spaces

Let $\varepsilon \to F_\varepsilon$ be a one-dimensional parametric submodel of $\mathcal{M}$, going through $F_X$ at $\varepsilon = 0$. Recall that the score vector of this submodel is defined as $s(X) = \frac{d}{d\varepsilon} \log f_\varepsilon(X) \in L_0^2(F_X)$. Here $L_0^2(F_X)$ is the Hilbert space of all functions of $X$ with mean zero and finite variance under $F_X$, and the tangent space $T(F_X)$ is defined as the linear closure of all possible scores in this Hilbert space. A very important space in efficiency theory is $T_{NUIS} \subset T$, called the nuisance tangent space, which is the linear closure in $L_0^2(F_X)$ of all scores of submodels $F_\varepsilon$ such that $\frac{d}{d\varepsilon} \mu(F_\varepsilon) = 0$. The interpretation of such submodels is that local fluctuations from the truth only change $\eta$ and not $\mu$. Finally, we define the orthogonal complement of the nuisance tangent space as $T_{NUIS}^\perp(F_X) = \{h \in L_0^2(F_X) : \langle h(X), s(X) \rangle = 0$ $\forall s(X) \in T_{NUIS}(F_X)\}$, where $\langle h(X), s(X) \rangle = E_{F_X}[h(X)^T s(X)]$ is the inner product of $h(X)$ and $s(X)$ in $L_0^2(F_X)$.

## Relationship Between Estimating Functions and Tangent Spaces

It has been shown by van der Laan and Robbins that in a very strong sense, the only estimating functions of interest are those that are members of $T_{NUIS}^\perp$. For such estimating functions $D(X \mid \mu, \eta)$, it can be shown that if $F_\varepsilon$ is a submodel whose score is in the nuisance tangent space, then $\frac{d}{d\varepsilon} E_{F_X}[D(X \mid \mu(F_\varepsilon), \eta(F_\varepsilon))] = 0$ at $\varepsilon = 0$. This property can be used to show that if $\hat{\eta}$ is consistent for $\eta$, then under regularity conditions the solution $\mu_n$ of $\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n D(X_i \mid \mu, \hat{\eta}) = 0$ is asymptotically linear for $\mu(F_X)$ with influence curve $IC = -[\frac{d}{d\varepsilon} E_{F_X}[D(X \mid \mu(F_X), \eta(F_X))]^{-1} D(X \mid \mu(F_X), \eta(F_X))$.

Another property of the nuisance tangent space $T_{NUIS}^\perp$ is that it contains the linear span of all components of all gradients. Here a gradient is a random variable $l(X)$ such that if $F_\varepsilon$ has score $s(X)$ then $\lim_{\varepsilon \to 0} \frac{1}{\varepsilon} (\mu(F_\varepsilon) - \mu(F_X)) = \langle l(X), s(X) \rangle$. In general there can be many different gradients, but the unique gradient in the tangent space $T(F_X)$ is called the canonical gradient. If an asymptotically linear estimator has an influence curve equal to the canonical gradient, then the estimator is efficient, meaning that it has better asymptotic performance than any other regular estimator.

## Example: Survival Analysis with no Censoring

Let $T \sim F$ be a survival time, where $\mathcal{M}$ is a completely nonparametric model. Here $F$ can be any cdf of a nonnegative random variable. Let $\mu(F) = F(t)$ be the parameter of interest, for fixed $t$. In this example there is no nuisance parameter $\eta$. Consider the parametric submodel $f_\varepsilon(T) = (1 + \varepsilon h(T))f(T)$, where $\int h(T)dF(T) = 0$ but $h$ is otherwise arbitrary. Note that the score of this submodel is $h(T)$, so the tangent space is all of $L_0^2(T)$, which immediately tells us that any asymptotically linear estimate is efficient because its influence curve must be in this tangent space. We now formally calculate $T_{NUIS}^\perp$, the orthogonal complement of the nuisance tangent space.

$$\left. \frac{d}{d\varepsilon} \mu(F_\varepsilon) \right|_{\varepsilon=0} = \lim_{\varepsilon \to 0} \frac{1}{\varepsilon} (\mu(F_\varepsilon) - \mu(F)) = \lim_{\varepsilon \to 0} \frac{1}{\varepsilon} \int_0^t (f_\varepsilon(T) - f(T)) dT$$

$$= \lim_{\varepsilon \to 0} \frac{1}{\varepsilon} \int_0^t \varepsilon h(T) f(T) dT = \int_0^t h(T) dF(T) = \int (I(T \le t) - F(t)) h(T) dF(T)$$

$$= \langle I(T \le t) - F(t), h(T) \rangle$$

Setting this derivative to zero and solving for $h$ gives the nuisance tangent space. Thus, $T_{NUIS} = \{h(T) \in L_0^2(T) : h(T) \perp I(T \le t) - F(t)\}$. Taking the orthogonal complement of this space gives that $T_{NUIS}^\perp = [I(T \le t) - F(t)]$, where $[\bullet]$ denotes the linear span. Hence, $D(T \mid \mu) = I(T \le t) - \mu$ is in $T_{NUIS}^\perp$, and it is an estimating function because it clearly has mean zero under the truth. Because $T_{NUIS}^\perp$ is the span of a single random variable, we can check that using any estimating function from this space gives the same estimator, which is just $\mu_n = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n I(T_i \le t)$. We conclude from our previous results that $\mu_n$ is asymptotically linear (which we already could see without any efficiency theory), and it is efficient because it is the unique estimating function estimate over all estimating functions in $T_{NUIS}^\perp$.

## Estimating functions in regression

Suppose

$$Y = m(Z \mid B) + \varepsilon$$

where $Y$ denote the outcome, $Z$ is the vector of covariates, and $B$ denote the regression parameters. Rewriting as $\varepsilon(B) = Y - m(Z \mid B)$, we assume that $E[K(\varepsilon \mid B) \mid Z] = 0$ for a given monotone increasing function $x \longrightarrow K(x)$. For example, when $K(\varepsilon) = \varepsilon$, we have $m(Z \mid B_0) = E[Y \mid Z]$; when $K(\varepsilon) = I(\varepsilon > 0) - 1/2$, we have $m(Z \mid B_0) = \text{Med}[Y \mid Z]$; when $K(\varepsilon) = I(\varepsilon > 0) - (1 - p)$, we have $m(Z \mid B_0) = p-\text{th}$ quantile of $Y \mid Z$.

Let us now define

$$D_h(Y, Z, B) = h(Z) K(\varepsilon(B))$$

to be the class of all estimating functions for $B$, and $B_n(h)$ be a solution of

$$0 = \sum_{i=1}^n D_h(Y_i, Z_i, B)$$

$$= \sum_{i=1}^n h(Z_i) K(Y_i - m(Z_i \mid B))$$

where $h(\cdot)$ can be any vector function.

Now,

$$B_n(h) - B_0 \approx \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n C^{-1}(h) D_h(Y_i, Z_i, B_0)$$

where $C(h) = -\left[ \frac{\delta}{\delta B} E_0 [h(Z) K(\varepsilon(B))] \right]$.

Let

$$h_{opt}(Z) = \frac{\frac{\delta}{\delta B} m(Z \mid B)}{\mathrm{Var}[K(\varepsilon) \mid Z]},$$

and $h_n$ be an estimator of $h_{opt}$ according to a (guessed) model of $E[K(\varepsilon)^2 \mid Z]$. If $B_n$ is a solution of

$$0 = \sum_{i=1}^n h_n(Z_i) K(\varepsilon_i(B)),$$

then $B_n - B_0 \approx \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n C^{-1}(h^*) h^*(Z_i) K(\varepsilon_i(B))$ where $h^*$ is the limit of $h$. In addition, note that $B_n$ is asymptotically linear, and is an efficient estimator of $B_0$ if $h_n \longrightarrow h_{opt}$.

## Right-censored data structure

Let $X(t)$ denote a time-dependent full data structure process of interest, and $T$ denote the endpoint of this process. A full data structure is defined as $X = \bar{X}(T) = (X(t) : t \le T)$. The observed data structure (what we can observe) is defined as $O = (\tilde{T} = \min(T, C), \Delta = I(T \le C), \bar{X}(\tilde{T}))$ where $C$ is a censoring variable. We denote the distribution of the observed data structure by $P_{F_X, G_{C|X}}$ where $G_{C|X}$ represents the distribution of the censoring mechanism.

Under CAR (Coarsening At Random) assumption, for $t < T$, we have

$$\lambda_C(t \mid X) = m(t, \bar{X}(t))$$

for some function $m$.

## 4 Right Censored Data Structure (Cont'd)

Let $X(t)$ denote the time-dependent full data process of interest, and $T$ be an endpoint of this process. Then the full data structure is defined as

$$X = \bar{X}(T) \equiv (X(t) : t \le T) = (X(s), s \le T) \sim F_X$$

We observe data $O = (\tilde{T} = \min(T, C), \Delta = I(T \le C), \bar{X}(\tilde{T})) = \phi(C, X)$, where $C$ is a censoring variable for a known $\phi$. Then we have $O \sim P_{F_X, G_{C|X}}$.  
The full data model: $F_X \in \mathcal{M}^F$.  
eg. $\mathcal{M}^F = \{F_X : E(\log T \mid X) = m(Z \mid \beta)\}$, $Z \in X(0)$  
Or if $\mathcal{M}^F$ is nonparametric, eg. (2). $\mathcal{M}^F = \{F_X : \lambda_{T|Z}(t \mid Z) = \lambda_0(t) e^{\beta Z}\}$.

To find the full data distribution, we need the parameter of interest: $\mu : \mathcal{M}^F \to \mathbb{R}^k$, eg.

$$\mu(F_X) = E_{F_X}(\log T \mid Z), \mu(F_X) = P_{F_X}(T > t_0), \mu(F_X) = \beta$$

CAR: for $t < T$, $\lambda_{C|X}(t \mid X) = m(t, \bar{X}(t))$ for some function $m$.  
Let $F_X$ be part of $f(o) = L_{F_X}(o) g(o \mid X)$, then the likelihood can be written as

$$L(F_X) = f_X(\bar{X}(T))^\Delta f_X(\bar{X}(\tilde{T}))^{1-\Delta} = [\prod_{t=0}^T P(X(t) \mid \bar{X}(t-))]^\Delta [\prod_{t=0}^{\tilde{T}} P(X(t) \mid \bar{X}(t-))]^{1-\Delta}$$

The content in the square bracket is the probability of seeing $X(t)$ given the past.

**Example:** Observed data $O : (\tilde{T}, \Delta, W)$, where $W$ is baseline covariates. By CAR, $C \perp T \mid W$.  
Let $\mathcal{M}^F = \text{nonparametric}$, $\mu(F_{T,W}) \equiv P(T > t_0)$. Then we can use Kaplan-Meier estimator $\hat{P}(T > t_0 \mid W = w)$: because $E_W P(T > t_0 \mid W) = P(T > t_0)$, then

$$\hat{P}(T > t_0) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \hat{P}(T > t_0 \mid W = w_i) = \sum_{j=1}^k \frac{n_j}{n} \hat{P}(T > t_0 \mid W = x_j)$$

when $W$ is discrete with outcome $x_1, \ldots, x_k$.  
However, when $W$ is continuous or has many categories, the situation will be much more complicated. By the curse of dimensionality, we can only construct sensible estimators of $\mu(F_X)$ by making model assumptions on either $\lambda_C(t \mid X)$ or $f_X(x)$.  
Define $A(t) = I(\tilde{T} \le t, \Delta = 0)$ which is a counting process of censoring. Then the partial likelihood is given by

$$L_G(\tilde{T}, \Delta, \bar{X}(\tilde{T})) = \prod_t^{\tilde{T}} E(\partial A(t) \mid \bar{X}(t), \bar{A}(t-))^{\partial A(t)} (1 - E(\partial A(t) \mid \bar{X}(t-), \bar{A}(t-)))^{1-\partial A(t)}$$

We can model the intensity of $A(t)$ w.r.t. $(\bar{X}_A(t), \bar{A}(t-))$.  
With a multiplicative intensity model:

$$E(\partial A(t) \mid \bar{A}(t-), \bar{X}(t)) = I(\tilde{T} \ge t) \lambda_0(t) e^{\alpha L(t)}$$

where $\lambda_0(t) e^{\alpha L(t)} = \Pr(C = t \mid C \ge t, \bar{X}(t))$. Then $L(t) = f(\bar{X}(t))$ for some function $f$, $X_A(t) = X(\min(t, \tilde{T}))$.  
If censoring $A(t)$ only jumps at discrete times $t_1 < t_2 < \cdots < t_M$, then using logistic model

## Notes re. Maximum Likelihood vs Previously Mentioned Method

- The Maximum Likelihood method factorizes the full data and censoring, but it does not care about censoring. This is equivalent to a Bayesian point of view where one does not care about the other part of the likelihood.
- We also know that the censoring is independent of survival and covariates. One who performs only the maximum likelihood method cannot do KM on all of those levels.
- The maximum likelihood is asymptotically efficient if it works, but the MLE in this case (when taking into account censoring and multiple covariates [with potentially many levels]) it is biased. This is referred to as the curse of dimensionality.
- The ML tries to be globally efficient and therefore it breaks down when the model becomes too high dimensional.
- KM within every cell unbiased and very variable. You increase the variance when you increase the dimensions.
- A person who performs the maximum likelihood method needs to model the error distribution. We do not have to assume a parametric model for the error distribution.
- Double Robust: If either the censoring model or likelihood is correct you get a consistent locally efficient estimator.

## Multiplicative Intensity Models
Matthew Sylvester  
April 28, 2004

**Counting Processes Data:** $(\tilde{T} = \min(T, C), \Delta = I(T \le C), \bar{X}(\tilde{T}))$, where $T$ is the endpoint, $C$ is the censoring time and $\bar{X}(\tilde{T})$ is any data that might be collected on a person until time $\tilde{T}$.

Suppose $X(t) = (N_1^*(t), \ldots, N_k^*(t), L(t))$,  
where $N_h(t)$ is a counting process, $h=1,\ldots,k$ denotes the index of that process and $*$ denotes that it is based on the full data. $L(t)$ is a time-dependent covariate process. Note that there might be several jumps when moving to the next state and that all counting processes stop jumping at $T$. That is, $N_h^*(t) = N_h^*(\min(t, T))$.

## Examples

1. Consider multiple counting processes

   $$N_h^*(t) = I(T_h \le t), \quad h = 1, \ldots, k$$

   where $T_1, \ldots, T_k$ refer to distinct counting processes (i.e. the time to certain events). For example, $T_1$ might refer to the time to AIDS while $T_2$ refers to the time to death. This might mean that the first process jumps when AIDS is contracted and that the second process jumps at death or $T$.

2. Now consider just one counting process

   $$N^*(t) = \sum_{j=1}^k I(T_j \le t)$$

   that jumps whenever the events occur. For example, for asthmatic children, $T_1$ might be the time to the first attack, $T_2$ might be the time to the second attack, etc.

3. Consider the Simplest Case

   $$N^*(t) = I(T \le t)$$

   that jumps at death.

## Observed Data

$$N_h(t) = N_h^*(\min(t, \tilde{T})), \text{ where } h = 1, \ldots, k$$

We have the history:

$$\mathcal{F}(t) = (\bar{X}(\min(t, \tilde{T})), \bar{A}(\min(t, \tilde{T})), A(t) = I(C \le t))$$

When $t = \infty$, we see the full data past.

**Multiplicative Intensity Models** Suppose we have coarsening at random (CAR). We can get an intensity with respect to history when we are trying to model the probability of a counting process jumping given the past:

$N_h$ with history $\mathcal{F}(t)$ :

$$E(\partial N_h(t) \mid \mathcal{F}(t)) \equiv \lambda_h(t \mid \mathcal{F}(t)),$$

For $t < T$,

$$\lambda_c(t \mid X) = m(t, \bar{X}(t)),$$

which is reasonable if censoring is only determined by the past.  
Then the intensity of the observed counting process is:

$$E(\partial N_h(t) \mid \mathcal{F}_t) = I(\tilde{T} \ge t) E(\partial N_h(t) \mid \mathcal{F}(t), \tilde{T} \ge t)$$

$$= I(\tilde{T} \ge t) E(\partial N_h^*(t) \mid \bar{X}(t), \tilde{T} \ge t, C \ge t)$$

$$\stackrel{\text{CAR}}{=} (I(\tilde{T} \ge t) E(\partial N_h^*(t) \mid \bar{X}(t), \tilde{T} \ge t)$$

where we are conditioning on the full data past, and the censoring only depends on the past. We are assuming censoring does not depend on covariates not included, but this assumption becomes weaker as more covariates are put in the past. Note that the multiplicative intensity model can only be applied to the individual counting processes, of which every subject might have several (failure, infection, etc.)

If there are no covariates, the baseline hazard of dying now given that the person has not died yet and censoring has not occurred yet is given by:

$$P(T = t \mid T \ge t, C \ge t)$$

which is what we would estimate with the Cox proportional hazards model with no covariates. If there is independent censoring, this reduces to $P(T = t \mid T \ge t)$.

Now, if we would like to estimate the intensity with respect to a subset of the past:

$$E(\partial N_h(t) \mid \bar{N}_h(t-), Z(t-)),$$

where $(N_h(t), Z(t) \subset X(t))$.

If censoring is independent of the past, this is consistent, but inefficient. If we have CAR for the original data, we can use IPCW:

$$\int h(t), \bar{Z}(t-)) \partial M(t) \frac{I(\tilde{T} \ge t)}{\bar{G}(t \mid X)}.$$

Or,

$$\int h(t), \bar{Z}(t-)) \partial M(t) \frac{I(\tilde{T} \ge t) \bar{G}(t \mid \bar{Z}(t))}{\bar{G}(t \mid X)}$$

where we use cox proportional hazards to model the hazard of censoring mechanism. However, even when it is known that this is one, we should still estimate because it is more efficient.

Now, when we are adjusting for the entire past, the IPCW is not necessary. We implement it when we have just $Z(t)$ where $Z(t)$ is not the whole past. For example, we might just have the treatment arm. Now, for the partial likelihood approach, we need to throw in everything that might be informative of censoring. We need to keep adjusting for confounding.

## More on Multiplicative Intensity Models
When the counting process is continuous(i.e. it can jump at any point in time), assume:

$$\lambda_h(t \mid \mathcal{F}(t-)) = Y_h(t) E(\partial N_h(t) \mid \mathcal{F}(t), Y_h(t) = 1)$$

$$= Y_h(t) \lambda_{0h}(t) \exp(\beta_h Z_h(t))$$

where $Y_h(t)$ is defined as the indicator that $N_h(t)$ is still at risk of jumping at time $t$, $\mathcal{F}(t)$ indicates the past, $\lambda_{0h}(t)$ indicates the baseline hazard, $Z_h(t)$ is a function of $\mathcal{F}(t)$, and is composed of covariates thought predictive of the counting process jumping, and $\beta_h$ denotes the regression coefficients.

For the special case of proportional hazards with one counting process and setting the history of censoring equal to $\bar{A}(\min(t, \tilde{T})$:

$$N(t) = I(\tilde{T} \le t, \Delta = 1)$$

$$\mathcal{F}(t) = (\bar{N}(t), W, \bar{A}(\min(t, \tilde{T}))$$

where we are only adjusting for the baseline covariates.

Then,

$$E(\partial N(t) \mid \mathcal{F}(t)) = I(\tilde{T} \ge t) \lambda_0(t) exp(\beta W)$$

$$= I(\tilde{T} \ge t)(\partial N(t) \mid T \ge t, C \ge t, W)$$

$$C \perp T \mid W$$

$$= P(T = t \mid T \ge t, W)$$

which is the Cox proportional hazards model. Then, Cox proportional hazards assumes that $\lambda_{T|W}(t \mid W) = \lambda_0(t) exp(\beta W)$, a proportional hazards assumption. The ratio of two will not be dependent on time, a restrictive assumption. Our method is more general, and we do not need to make this assumption. Then $W$ can be a function of time. This means that we can do data-adaptive work by pluggin on other basis functions for $W$, etc.

## Maximum Likelihood Estimation
We are interested in estimating the baseline hazards and coefficients $\beta$.

Give every counting process its own covariates. Then, we can create a long vector that has the real values when counting process 1 occurs and 0's when counting process 2 occurs, for example.

$$\lambda_h(t \mid \mathcal{F}(t-)) = Y_h(t) \lambda_{0h}(t) exp(\beta Z_h(t)),$$

where we choose the covariate so that it reduces to what is wanted.

**Example** We have $\beta_1 W_1$ and $\beta_2 W_2$.  
Then, set $Z_1 = (W_1, 0)$, $Z_2 = (0, W_2)$, and $\beta = (\beta_1, \beta_2)$  
We then have,

$$\beta^T Z_1 = (\beta_1 \beta_2) \begin{pmatrix} W_1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} = \beta_1 W_1$$

$$\beta^T Z_2 = (\beta_1 \beta_2) \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ W_2 \end{pmatrix} = \beta_2 W_2$$

The partial likelihood of $(N_1, \ldots, N_k)$ with respect to $\mathcal{F}(t-)$ is defined as:

$$L_P(\Lambda_h, \beta \mid \mathcal{F}(\text{inf})) = \prod_t \prod_{h=1}^k \lambda_h(t \mid \mathcal{F}(t))^{\partial N_h(t)} (1 - \lambda_\cdot(t \mid \mathcal{F}(t-))^{1 - \partial N_\cdot(t)}$$

where:

$$N_\cdot(t) \equiv \sum_{h=1}^k N_h(t)$$

and

$$\lambda_\cdot(t \mid \mathcal{F}(t-)) = E(\partial N_\cdot(t) \mid \mathcal{F}(t-)) = \sum_{h=1}^k \lambda_h(t \mid \mathcal{F}(t-))$$

If something jumps, we use the intensity of the counting process; otherwise, we use one minus the intensity.

So, for the maximum likelihood estimate over the parameter fixing the coefficients and maximizing over the baseline hazards:

$$L_P(\Lambda_h, \beta \mid O_1, \ldots, O_n) = \prod_{i=1}^n \prod_t \prod_{h=1}^k \lambda_h(t \mid \mathcal{F}(t))^{\partial N_h(t)} (1 - \lambda_i(t \mid \mathcal{F}(t-))^{1 - \partial N_i(t)}$$

and only keep track of counting processes at time $t$ where $O_i$, $i = 1 \ldots n$ are the observations.
